extracted.intended_audience: students and scholars of humour studies (philosophy, sociology, psychology) and cultural critics
extracted.subtask_description: Framework and evaluative criteria for analysing humour (jokes, laughter, ridicule) in their social, political, developmental, and rhetorical contexts. Emphasises what good critique/theory should attend to and common omissions to avoid.

rubrics_metrics.name: Account for both verbal and non-verbal humour
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not confine analysis to verbal jokes; distinguish between 'a joke is made' and 'the comic is found' and recognise that comic actions (exaggerated gestures, slips, clowning) can be deliberately produced.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Freud separated joke and comic but overstated the distinction; analysts should treat non-verbal comic performances as potentially deliberately created (e.g., professional clowns) rather than merely 'found'. Consider Bergson's contributions on comic actions when integrating non-verbal humour.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid reducing humour to a single cause
rubrics_metrics.description: Theory should not claim one psychological cause (superiority, incongruity, or relief) explains all humour phenomena.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The chapter recommends recognising humour's paradoxical nature and combining explanatory factors rather than insisting on unitary causes; test theories against the three paradoxes (universal/particular; social/anti-social; mysterious/analyzable).

rubrics_metrics.name: Attend to the social and disciplinary functions of ridicule
rubrics_metrics.description: Analyse how ridicule can operate to discipline, teach, enforce social codes, as well as to mock or rebel.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Bergson's view that laughter disciplines social life should be integrated with Freudian skepticism; do not automatically treat ridicule as merely negative or merely subversive (historical examples: Plato, Shaftesbury).

rubrics_metrics.name: Treat humour as a social act — analyse reception
rubrics_metrics.description: Evaluate humour not just by intent or form but by how audiences receive it; jokes require an audience to complete their pleasure-producing function.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use episodes like Berlusconi in the European Parliament to show mismatches between intent and reception. Success/failure of humour should be analysed in social context; 'humour' can be present even if it fails to elicit laughter.

rubrics_metrics.name: Take negative, political and ethical dimensions of humour seriously
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not let 'ideological positivism' erase mockery, offensive, or harmful humour from theoretical consideration; analyse morally problematic humour as part of humour studies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Critics should avoid defining humour only as positive or benign. Treat offensive mockery (e.g., concentration-camp quips) as legitimate objects of analysis rather than dismissing them to preserve a comforting view of humour.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish 'pure aggression' jokes from stereotype-based jokes
rubrics_metrics.description: Recognise jokes that do not attribute qualities to a target but invite aggression (the 'tiling joke' / 'three at the bottom of a river') and treat these as a distinct class.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Academics often ignore non-stereotyping violent jokes, but they can be common (e.g., KKK sites) and should be analysed for their aggressive dynamics and social effects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assess the relationship between humour and actual violence/power
rubrics_metrics.description: Determine whether a joke treats violence as an abstract inappropriate idea or as actual violence made a matter for laughter; evaluate implications for victims and social consequences.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compare 'lawyer' versions (satirical, disproportionate fantasy) with racist versions (which laugh about real, occurring violence); when jokes normalize or celebrate real violence they have different ethical and social standing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consider performer/audience positionality (insider vs outsider)
rubrics_metrics.description: Analyse who tells the joke and their social position — outsider groups may use conventional joke-forms to normalise violence; insider jokes function differently.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The same joke form (e.g., 'bottom of the river') takes different meanings when told about lawyers vs racial others; examine power/status of tellers and audience to interpret intent and effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Incorporate developmental origins and learning of humour
rubrics_metrics.description: Trace childhood roots of adult humour and examine how laughter is taught and learned (parents laughing at children, mockery as instruction).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Freud's emphasis on infantile roots is valuable; also consider Bergson's disciplinary angle — parents' tendentious laughter may teach children social codes and how to laugh.

rubrics_metrics.name: Treat laughter as rhetorical and learned, not merely biological
rubrics_metrics.description: View laughter as part of rhetorical communication that must be learnt and taught, with moral, political and aesthetic dimensions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reject simplistic biological accounts that equate physiological laughter with having a 'sense of humour'. Analyse 'unlaughter' (the rhetorical refusal to laugh) as meaningful in interaction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not define humour solely by elicited laughter
rubrics_metrics.description: Humour should not be defined only as that which provokes laughter; its identity can persist even when it fails to produce laughter or when other effects (insult, silence, humiliation) are the aim.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess aims beyond amusement — e.g., Berlusconi's remark was intended to humiliate/silence, not necessarily to make the target laugh. Evaluate success relative to intended social/political ends.

rubrics_metrics.name: Analyse meta-discourse around humour (claims of irony, apology, reframing)
rubrics_metrics.description: Examine how speakers and audiences comment on humour after the fact (e.g., claiming 'it was ironic') and how such framing affects moral/aesthetic judgement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When humour goes wrong, the ensuing meta-discourse reveals disputes over appropriateness and intent; study reframing moves (ironising, regretting vs apologising).

rubrics_metrics.name: Question relief/physiological explanations when they ignore tendentious motives
rubrics_metrics.description: Be cautious about purely physiological relief accounts of laughter (nervous energy discharge) that sidestep possible tendentious/aggressive motives behind laughter.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Freud's adoption of relief theory for the comic is critiqued here for underplaying aggression; analyse whether laughter involves empathy or concealed hostility in each case.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evaluate explanatory scope: why some incongruities provoke laughter and others do not
rubrics_metrics.description: A good theory must explain selective humour response — why apparently similar incongruities sometimes provoke laughter and sometimes fail.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Test theories against empirical variability; do not rely solely on internal psychological descriptions without social context to account for differential reception.

rubrics_metrics.name: Handle biological/primatological data cautiously — distinguish capacity to laugh from 'sense of humour'
rubrics_metrics.description: Recognise that physiological or primate laughter-like responses (e.g., tickling apes) do not equate to human humour which is language-linked and culturally learned.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use comparative data to inform questions of evolution and capacity, but avoid conflating acoustic or reflexive sounds with socially constructed humour; emphasise the role of language and teaching in human humour.
